Sources hiding on the light cone

June 2026 · based on arXiv:2606.27241

Symmetry can hand you an exact solution of a hard nonlinear field equation almost for free. Reduce Yang–Mills theory along the orbits of the Lorentz group and the equations collapse to a small mechanical system whose solutions you can write down. The catch is what happens at the boundary between the orbits — the light cone — where the otherwise-smooth field develops a singular stress tensor.

The natural instinct is to smooth it: shift a denominator slightly and the singularity should melt into something regular. It does not. A real shift only moves the support onto a hyperboloid, and on such a surface a finite-order completion cannot be made simultaneously conserved and traceless — the two properties a physical source must have. Both can hold at once only on the characteristic null cone itself.

On that cone the completion is essentially unique: a fixed even core plus a single residual mode, carrying a genuine future/past asymmetry — a cone-charge that the geometry forces rather than one you put in by hand. The lesson is structural: whether a singular stress tensor admits a clean source depends not on how rough it looks, but on the kind of surface it lives on. The principal symbol, not the regulator, decides.

The full account — shifted-shell precursors, the conormal obstruction, the matching law, and the cone-charge response — is in the preprint arXiv:2606.27241.

Dr. Kaushlendra Kumar · Queen Mary University of London
